newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn parliament blesses Czech reconciliation pact.
newsitem.headline: Bonn parliament blesses Czech reconciliation pact.

text.p: The German parliament on Thursday approved a declaration of reconciliation with the Czech Republic intended to set aside lingering resentments more than five decades after the end of World War Two.
An overwhelming majority in the lower house gave their blessing to the agreement, which was signed last week by Chancellor Helmut Kohl and Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus.

There were 578 votes in favour, 20 against and 23 abstentions. In the declaration, Bonn expresses sorrow for the 1938-45 Nazi occupation of the Czech lands, and Prague its regret for the post-war expulsion of 2.5 million ethnic Germans.

"It is not a matter of saying that this episode of our history has been put to rest. It was and is about speaking openly about those issues, which could make our common future difficult," Kohl told deputies in a parliamentary debate.

"This declaration should however -- with all respect to hurt feelings -- make a contribution to reconciliation. It should help to break out of the vicious circle of settling scores and mutual recriminations," Kohl said.
It took two years of delicate talks to draw up the final text, which is still controversial in both countries. In the Czech Republic, far-right Republicans and communists oppose it.

In Germany, the Sudeten Germans -- survivors and relatives of those were expelled after the war -- are angry that they were not included in the negotiations and that the agreement fails to provide for compensation for confiscated property.
Kohl called on the Sudeten Germans to accept the accord.
In the declaration, Germany also expresses its support for Czech membership of the European Union and the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation.
